opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of my conviction came from arguing with my advisor. They came from a very classical robotics background: modeling, planning, control, carefully engineered state estimation. Their instinct was always, "If you understand the physics well enough, you can write down the right model and the right controller."

I respected that a lot, and I still do. But in our discussions I kept noticing where that approach broke down. Whenever we moved from a clean lab setup to something messy, like deformable objects, cluttered scenes, or contact-rich manipulation, the modeling effort exploded. Every new task meant a new set of assumptions and hand-tuned parameters, and a lot of graduate-student time. My advisor would say, "That's just the cost of doing it right." I started to feel that the cost itself was the signal. If every new task needs a human expert to rebuild the pipeline, it doesn't scale.

What was valuable, though, was that my advisor pushed back hard on the hype. They'd ask, "Okay, your learned policy works. Why does it work? When will it fail? What's the data actually teaching it?" That forced me to be much more rigorous. I couldn't just say "neural networks will figure it out." I had to think about data coverage, generalization, and where structure still matters.

So the conviction formed somewhat through opposition. The classical view made me see clearly what learning could replace: the endless per-task engineering. It also taught me what learning shouldn't throw away: good hardware intuition, an understanding of physics, and careful evaluation. By the end I wasn't betting on machine learning because it was trendy. I was betting on it because I'd seen up close how far the traditional approach could go and where it hit a wall.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the conviction formed through discussions and opposition from the advisor, which clarified what learning could replace and why Kay was betting on it.

r002.rationale: The candidate criticizes traditional methods for requiring a human expert to rebuild the pipeline for each new task, saying that dependence does not scale.

fable-5.1.text:
It's funny, because my advisor was about as traditional as it gets. Very classical: dynamics, control theory, model everything explicitly, prove stability. And I came in around the time deep learning was starting to show results in vision, and I remember bringing him a paper and saying, look, what if we just let the robot learn this from data? And his reaction was basically, that's not engineering, that's hoping.

And honestly, for a while I thought he was right. Because when you're sitting in a lab with a real arm, and you try to apply some learning method, it's brittle. It breaks. You spend three weeks collecting data and the policy does something stupid the moment the lighting changes. Meanwhile his approach, with a good model and a good controller, just works, every single time, as long as the world looks like the model.

But that last part was the thing I kept getting stuck on. As long as the world looks like the model. We'd have these long arguments, sometimes in his office, sometimes in the lab at midnight, and I'd push him: okay, but what happens when it's not a rigid block on a table? What happens when it's a cable, or a piece of cloth, or a drawer that sticks a little? And he would admit, you'd have to re-model it. Every time. By a person. And I remember thinking, that doesn't scale. That's a system where the bottleneck is always the number of PhD students you have.

So the conviction didn't come from him being wrong. It actually came from him being rigorous. He forced me to be honest about where learning was failing, and that made me very clear about what problem it actually had to solve: not replacing control, but replacing the human who writes the model. Once I framed it that way, the brittleness stopped looking like a dead end and started looking like a data problem, a scale problem. Those are solvable. The modeling-by-hand problem is not.

He still teases me about it. But I think the reason I ended up believing in learning-based robots so strongly is precisely that I had to defend it against someone who really knew why it shouldn't work.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated arguments with the advisor and says defending learning against his rigorous objections clarified why Kay believed in learning-based robots.

r002.rationale: It criticizes traditional methods for requiring people to re-model each new object or situation, calling the human modeling bottleneck unscalable.

astra-6.text: Those discussions pushed me to make the argument more concrete: what does learning actually give a robot that we can’t achieve by explicitly designing its behavior? Traditional robotics gives you a lot of structure and control, and you shouldn’t dismiss that. But when you think about a robot operating in an unfamiliar environment, it becomes difficult to anticipate every situation and write down every rule. That’s where I saw the potential for machine learning—to let the robot improve through experience. The challenge from my advisor helped sharpen that conviction: learning had to earn its place by solving problems that the existing approach struggled with.

r001.rationale: The response says the discussions and advisor’s challenge pushed Kay to make the case concrete and sharpened her conviction by clarifying what learning could solve.

r002.rationale: It says traditional robotics relies on structure, control, and explicitly written rules, but does not criticize excessive reliance on human experts.

sol-6.1.text:
Those discussions pushed me to be more precise about what I believed machine learning could contribute. Traditional robotics has a lot of powerful tools, so simply saying, “We’ll learn everything from data,” isn’t a convincing answer. You have to explain where learning helps and how you’ll know it works.

For me, the central question became how a robot handles situations you haven’t explicitly designed for. You can build a very capable system for a controlled environment, but the real world keeps introducing variation. That strengthened my conviction that learning needed to be part of the solution. It also made me more careful: the goal is to combine learning with the structure and engineering discipline that robotics already has.

r001.rationale: The response says the discussions pushed Kay to clarify what he believed machine learning could contribute and strengthened his conviction that learning needed to be part of the solution.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the limits of controlled environments and the value of combining learning with robotics engineering, but does not criticize traditional robotics for relying too heavily on human experts.
